questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A neutron star possesses a density equivalent to that of nuclear matter. Assuming the star is spherical, determine the radius of a neutron star with a mass of $4.0 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$ (twice the mass of the sun).
questions.solution:
The density of nuclear matter is approximately $\rho \approx 3 \times 10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3$.

Given the mass of the neutron star, $M = 4.0 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$.

Assuming the neutron star is spherical, its density is given by:

$\rho = \dfrac{M}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$

Rearranging for the radius $R$:

$R^3 = \dfrac{3M}{4\pi \rho}$

Substituting the values:

$R^3 = \dfrac{3 \times 4.0 \times 10^{30}}{4\pi \times 3 \times 10^{17}}$

$R^3 = \dfrac{10^{13}}{\pi} \approx 3.18 \times 10^{12} \text{ m}^3$

Taking the cube root:

$R \approx 1.47 \times 10^4 \text{ m} \approx 15 \text{ km}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the amount of energy released during the reaction given below:
$^{7}\text{Li} + p \to \alpha + \alpha$.
The atomic mass of $^{7}\text{Li}$ is $7.0160 \text{ u}$ and that of $^{4}\text{He}$ is $4.0026 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction can be written using atomic masses as:

$^{7}\text{Li} + ^{1}\text{H} \rightarrow 2 ^{4}\text{He}$

Taking the atomic mass of hydrogen $^{1}\text{H}$ as $1.00783 \text{ u}$, the total mass of the reactants is:

$m_{\text{reactants}} = m(^{7}\text{Li}) + m(^{1}\text{H})$

$m_{\text{reactants}} = 7.0160 \text{ u} + 1.00783 \text{ u} = 8.02383 \text{ u}$

The total mass of the products is:

$m_{\text{products}} = 2 \times m(^{4}\text{He})$

$m_{\text{products}} = 2 \times 4.0026 \text{ u} = 8.0052 \text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is:

$\Delta m = m_{\text{reactants}} - m_{\text{products}}$

$\Delta m = 8.02383 \text{ u} - 8.0052 \text{ u} = 0.01863 \text{ u}$

The energy released $Q$ is calculated by converting the mass defect into energy (using $1 \text{ u} \approx 931 \text{ MeV}/c^2$):

$Q = 0.01863 \times 931 \text{ MeV} \approx 17.34 \text{ MeV}$

Answer: $17.34 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the binding energy per nucleon of $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$, given that its atomic mass is $196.96 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
Mass of a hydrogen atom, $m_H = 1.007825 \text{ u}$

Mass of a neutron, $m_n = 1.008665 \text{ u}$

Number of protons in $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$, $Z = 79$

Number of neutrons, $N = A - Z = 197 - 79 = 118$

Mass defect, $\Delta m = Z m_H + N m_n - M$

$\Delta m = 79 \times 1.007825 + 118 \times 1.008665 - 196.96$

$\Delta m = 79.618175 + 119.02247 - 196.96$

$\Delta m = 198.640645 - 196.96 = 1.680645 \text{ u}$

Total binding energy, $E_b = \Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV}$

$E_b = 1.680645 \times 931.5 \approx 1565.52 \text{ MeV}$

Binding energy per nucleon, $E_{bn} = \dfrac{E_b}{A}$

$E_{bn} = \dfrac{1565.52}{197} \approx 7.94 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Compute the energy released if an $\alpha$-particle is emitted by $^{238}\text{U}$. The atomic masses of $^{238}\text{U}$, $^{234}\text{Th}$, and $^{4}\text{He}$ are $238.0508 \text{ u}$, $234.04363 \text{ u}$, and $4.00260 \text{ u}$ respectively.
questions.solution:
The reaction for $\alpha$-decay is given by:

$^{238}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}\text{Th} + ^{4}\text{He} + Q$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is calculated as:

$\Delta m = m(^{238}\text{U}) - [m(^{234}\text{Th}) + m(^{4}\text{He})]$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta m = 238.0508 \text{ u} - (234.04363 \text{ u} + 4.00260 \text{ u})$

$\Delta m = 238.0508 \text{ u} - 238.04623 \text{ u} = 0.00457 \text{ u}$

The energy released $Q$ is:

$Q = \Delta m \times 931 \text{ MeV/u}$

$Q = 0.00457 \times 931 \text{ MeV} \approx 4.255 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose that the mass of a nucleus is roughly given by $M = A m_p$, where $A$ represents the mass number. Estimate the density of matter inside a nucleus in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, and determine the specific gravity of nuclear matter.
questions.solution:
The mass of the nucleus is given by $M = A m_p$, where $A$ is the mass number and $m_p \approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.

The radius of the nucleus is $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$.

The volume of the nucleus is:

$V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3 A$

The density of nuclear matter is:

$\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{A m_p}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{m_p}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3}$

Substituting the standard values:

$\rho = \dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi (1.1 \times 10^{-15})^3} \approx 3 \times 10^{17} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$

The specific gravity is the ratio of the density of the nuclear matter to the density of water ($\rho_w = 10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$):

$\text{Specific gravity} = \dfrac{\rho}{\rho_w} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{17}}{10^3} = 3 \times 10^{14}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the mass of an $\alpha$-particle, given that its binding energy is $28.2 \text{ MeV}$.
questions.solution:
The $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus, which consists of $2$ protons and $2$ neutrons.

Mass of a proton, $m_p \approx 1.00727 \text{ u}$
Mass of a neutron, $m_n \approx 1.00866 \text{ u}$

The total mass of the constituent nucleons is:
$M_{\text{nucleons}} = 2m_p + 2m_n$
$M_{\text{nucleons}} = 2(1.00727 \text{ u}) + 2(1.00866 \text{ u})$
$M_{\text{nucleons}} = 2.01454 \text{ u} + 2.01732 \text{ u} = 4.03186 \text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is related to the binding energy (BE) by the relation:
$\Delta m = \dfrac{\text{BE}}{931.5 \text{ MeV/u}}$
$\Delta m = \dfrac{28.2 \text{ MeV}}{931.5 \text{ MeV/u}} \approx 0.03027 \text{ u}$

The mass of the $\alpha$-particle is the total mass of the nucleons minus the mass defect:
$M_{\alpha} = M_{\text{nucleons}} - \Delta m$
$M_{\alpha} = 4.03186 \text{ u} - 0.03027 \text{ u} = 4.00159 \text{ u} \approx 4.0016 \text{ u}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Compute the energy that needs to be supplied to $^{238}\text{U}$ in order for two protons and two neutrons to be emitted one by one. The atomic masses of $^{238}\text{U}$, $^{234}\text{Th}$, and $^{4}\text{He}$ are $238.0508 \text{ u}$, $234.04363 \text{ u}$, and $4.00260 \text{ u}$ respectively.
questions.solution:
The process of emitting two protons and two neutrons is equivalent to breaking the $^{238}\text{U}$ nucleus into a $^{234}\text{Th}$ nucleus, 2 protons, and 2 neutrons.

The overall reaction is:
$^{238}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}\text{Th} + 2 ^{1}\text{H} + 2 ^{1}\text{n}$

Here, the mass of a hydrogen atom ($m_H$) is used instead of a bare proton to account for the electron mass, since the given masses of $^{238}\text{U}$ and $^{234}\text{Th}$ are atomic masses.

Using the standard masses $m_H = 1.007825 \text{ u}$ and $m_n = 1.008665 \text{ u}$, the total mass of the products is:
$M_{\text{products}} = M(^{234}\text{Th}) + 2m_H + 2m_n$
$M_{\text{products}} = 234.04363 + 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) = 238.07661 \text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ for the process is:
$\Delta m = M_{\text{products}} - M(^{238}\text{U})$
$\Delta m = 238.07661 - 238.0508 = 0.02581 \text{ u}$

The required energy is obtained by converting the mass defect into energy using $1 \text{ u} = 931 \text{ MeV}$:
$\Delta E = 0.02581 \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 24.029 \text{ MeV} \approx 24.03 \text{ MeV}$

Although the mass of $^{4}\text{He}$ is provided, it cancels out when combining the energy of alpha emission and the binding energy of the alpha particle, making it redundant for the overall calculation.

Answer: $24.03 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Calculate the energy released in the nuclear reaction $^{223}\text{Ra} \to ^{209}\text{Pb} + ^{14}\text{C}$. The necessary atomic masses are provided below.
$^{223}\text{Ra}$$^{209}\text{Pb}$$^{14}\text{C}$
$223.018 \text{ u}$$208.981 \text{ u}$$14.003 \text{ u}$
questions.solution:
The mass defect $\Delta m$ in the given nuclear reaction is calculated as:

$\Delta m = M(^{223}\text{Ra}) - [M(^{209}\text{Pb}) + M(^{14}\text{C})]$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta m = 223.018 - (208.981 + 14.003)$

$\Delta m = 223.018 - 222.984 = 0.034 \text{ u}$

The energy released $Q$ is given by:

$Q = \Delta m \times 931 \text{ MeV/u}$

$Q = 0.034 \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 31.654 \text{ MeV}$

This is approximately $31.65 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Evaluate the minimum energy required to separate a proton from a nucleus containing $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons. Let $M_{Z, N}$ denote the mass of an atom with $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons in the nucleus, and $M_H$ denote the mass of a hydrogen atom. This energy is termed the proton-separation energy.
options: $\Delta E = (M_{Z, N-1} + M_H - M_{Z, N}) c^2$
$\Delta E = (M_{Z, N} - M_{Z-1, N} - M_H) c^2$
$\Delta E = (M_{Z-1, N} + M_{Z, N} - M_H) c^2$
$\Delta E = (M_{Z-1, N} + M_H - M_{Z, N}) c^2$
questions.solution:
The separation of a proton from a nucleus with $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons can be represented as:

Nucleus$(Z, N) \rightarrow$ Nucleus$(Z-1, N) +$ proton

The minimum energy required for this process is the proton-separation energy, given by the mass difference between the products and the reactant:

$\Delta E = [m_{nuc}(Z-1, N) + m_p - m_{nuc}(Z, N)] c^2$

The nuclear mass $m_{nuc}$ can be expressed in terms of the atomic mass $M$ by subtracting the mass of the electrons:

$m_{nuc}(Z, N) = M_{Z, N} - Z m_e$

$m_{nuc}(Z-1, N) = M_{Z-1, N} - (Z-1) m_e$

Substituting these into the energy equation:

$\Delta E = [M_{Z-1, N} - (Z-1) m_e + m_p - (M_{Z, N} - Z m_e)] c^2$

$\Delta E = [M_{Z-1, N} + m_p + m_e - M_{Z, N}] c^2$

Since the mass of a hydrogen atom is $M_H = m_p + m_e$ (neglecting the small electronic binding energy), we get:

$\Delta E = (M_{Z-1, N} + M_H - M_{Z, N}) c^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the minimum energy required to separate a neutron from a nucleus containing $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons, in terms of the masses $M_{Z, N}$, $M_{Z, N-1}$, and the mass of the neutron $m_n$.
questions.solution:
The process of separating a neutron from a nucleus containing $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons can be represented by the nuclear reaction:

_{Z}^{Z+N}X \rightarrow _{Z}^{Z+N-1}Y + _{0}^{1}n$

The mass of the initial nucleus is $M_{Z, N}$.

The mass of the products is the sum of the mass of the residual nucleus and the mass of the neutron, which is $M_{Z, N-1} + m_n$.

The minimum energy required to separate the neutron is equal to the mass difference between the products and the initial nucleus, multiplied by $c^2$.

$\Delta m = \text{Mass of products} - \text{Mass of reactant}$

$\Delta m = M_{Z, N-1} + m_n - M_{Z, N}$

$\text{Energy required} = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = (M_{Z, N-1} + m_n - M_{Z, N}) c^2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $^{32}\text{P}$ undergoes beta-decay to $^{32}\text{S}$. Calculate the sum of the energy of the antineutrino and the kinetic energy of the $\beta$-particle. Disregard the recoil of the daughter nucleus. The atomic mass of $^{32}\text{P}$ is $31.974 \text{ u}$ and that of $^{32}\text{S}$ is $31.972 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The beta-decay equation is:

$^{32}_{15}\text{P} \rightarrow ^{32}_{16}\text{S} + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}$

The total energy released ($Q$-value) in the $\beta^{-}$-decay is shared between the $\beta$-particle, the antineutrino, and the recoiling daughter nucleus. Disregarding the recoil energy of the daughter nucleus, the sum of the kinetic energy of the $\beta$-particle and the energy of the antineutrino is equal to the $Q$-value.

The $Q$-value for $\beta^{-}$-decay in terms of atomic masses is:

$Q = [m(^{32}\text{P}) - m(^{32}\text{S})]c^2$

Substituting the given atomic masses:

$\Delta m = 31.974 - 31.972 = 0.002 \text{ u}$

Converting the mass defect into energy using $1 \text{ u} = 931.5 \text{ MeV}/c^2$:

$Q = 0.002 \times 931.5 \text{ MeV} = 1.863 \text{ MeV}$

The sum of the energy of the antineutrino and the kinetic energy of the $\beta$-particle is approximately $1.86 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A free neutron undergoes beta-decay to a proton, having a half-life of $14 \text{ minutes}$. Determine the decay constant.
questions.solution:
Given half-life $T_{1/2} = 14 \text{ minutes}$.

Converting to seconds:

$T_{1/2} = 14 \times 60 \text{ s} = 840 \text{ s}$

The relation between decay constant $\lambda$ and half-life is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$

Substituting the values:

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{840}$

$\lambda = 8.25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A free neutron undergoes beta-decay to a proton, having a half-life of $14 \text{ minutes}$. Calculate the energy liberated during this process.
questions.solution:
The beta-decay of a free neutron is represented by the equation:

$n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}$

The energy liberated ($Q$-value) during this process is given by the mass defect:

$Q = (m_{n} - m_{p} - m_{e})c^{2}$

Using the standard rest mass energies:
Rest mass energy of neutron, $m_{n}c^{2} = 939.565 \text{ MeV}$
Rest mass energy of proton, $m_{p}c^{2} = 938.272 \text{ MeV}$
Rest mass energy of electron, $m_{e}c^{2} = 0.511 \text{ MeV}$

Substituting these values:

$Q = 939.565 - 938.272 - 0.511$

$Q = 0.782 \text{ MeV}$

$Q = 782 \text{ keV}$

The half-life of $14 \text{ minutes}$ is extra information not required for this calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the missing product to complete the given decay scheme:
$^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \to \alpha + \,?$
questions.solution:
The given decay process is an alpha decay, which can be represented as:

$^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + ^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$

Applying the law of conservation of mass number:

$226 = 4 + A$

$A = 222$

Applying the law of conservation of atomic number:

$88 = 2 + Z$

$Z = 86$

The element with atomic number $86$ is Radon ($\text{Rn}$).

Thus, the missing product is $^{222}_{86}\text{Rn}$.

questions.q:
Determine the missing products to complete the given decay scheme:
$^{25}_{13}\text{Al} \to ^{25}_{12}\text{Mg} + \,?$
questions.solution:
The given nuclear reaction is $^{25}_{13} ext{Al} o ^{25}_{12} ext{Mg} + \,?$

In this decay, the mass number $A$ remains constant at $25$, while the atomic number $Z$ decreases from $13$ to $12$.

This indicates that a proton is converted into a neutron, which is characteristic of $ eta^{+}$ decay (positron emission).

The fundamental process for $ eta^{+}$ decay is $p o n + e^{+} + u$, where $e^{+}$ is a positron and $ u$ is an electron neutrino.

The complete decay equation is $^{25}_{13} ext{Al} o ^{25}_{12} ext{Mg} + e^{+} + u$.

The missing products are $e^{+}$ and $ u$.

questions.q: Potassium-40 can decay in three modes. It can decay via $\beta^{-}$-emission, $\beta^{+}$-emission or electron capture. Determine the equations showing the end products for these three modes respectively.
questions.solution:
In $ eta^{-}$ decay, a neutron is converted into a proton, emitting an electron ($e^{-}$) and an antineutrino ($ ar{ u}$). The atomic number increases by $1$.

$^{40}_{19} ext{K} o ^{40}_{20} ext{Ca} + e^{-} + ar{ u}$

In $ eta^{+}$ decay, a proton is converted into a neutron, emitting a positron ($e^{+}$) and a neutrino ($ u$). The atomic number decreases by $1$.

$^{40}_{19} ext{K} o ^{40}_{18} ext{Ar} + e^{+} + u$

In electron capture, an inner orbital electron is captured by the nucleus, converting a proton into a neutron and emitting a neutrino ($ u$). The atomic number decreases by $1$.

$^{40}_{19} ext{K} + e^{-} o ^{40}_{18} ext{Ar} + u$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Potassium-40 can decay in three modes: $\beta^{-}$-emission, $\beta^{+}$-emission or electron capture. The atomic masses of $^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}$, $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$ and $^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}$ are $39.9624 \text{ u}$, $39.9640 \text{ u}$ and $39.9626 \text{ u}$ respectively. Compute the $Q$-values for each of the three decay modes respectively.
questions.solution:
The $Q$-value for $\beta^{-}$-emission is given by the difference in atomic masses of the parent and daughter nuclei:

$Q_{\beta^{-}} = [M(^{40}_{19}\text{K}) - M(^{40}_{20}\text{Ca})] c^2$

Using $1 \text{ u} = 931 \text{ MeV}/c^2$, we get:

$Q_{\beta^{-}} = (39.9640 - 39.9626) \times 931 = 0.0014 \times 931 = 1.3034 \text{ MeV}$

The $Q$-value for $\beta^{+}$-emission accounts for the mass of two electrons (one from the positron emitted and one from the difference in atomic electron count):

$Q_{\beta^{+}} = [M(^{40}_{19}\text{K}) - M(^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}) - 2m_e] c^2$

Using $m_e c^2 = 0.511 \text{ MeV}$, we get:

$Q_{\beta^{+}} = (39.9640 - 39.9624) \times 931 - 2(0.511) = 0.0016 \times 931 - 1.022 = 1.4896 - 1.022 = 0.4676 \text{ MeV}$

The $Q$-value for electron capture is given by:

$Q_{EC} = [M(^{40}_{19}\text{K}) - M(^{40}_{18}\text{Ar})] c^2$

$Q_{EC} = (39.9640 - 39.9624) \times 931 = 0.0016 \times 931 = 1.4896 \text{ MeV} \approx 1.490 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Lithium ($Z = 3$) possesses two stable isotopes, $^{6}\text{Li}$ and $^{7}\text{Li}$. When a lithium sample is bombarded with neutrons, electrons and $\alpha$-particles are ejected. Identify the correct set of nuclear processes taking place.
questions.solution:
When a lithium sample containing $^{6}_{3}\text{Li}$ and $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ is bombarded with neutrons, the following nuclear reactions occur:

First, $^{6}_{3}\text{Li}$ captures a neutron to form the stable isotope $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$:

$^{6}_{3}\text{Li} + n \rightarrow ^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$

Next, $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ captures another neutron to form the radioactive isotope $^{8}_{3}\text{Li}$:

$^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + n \rightarrow ^{8}_{3}\text{Li}$

Since $^{8}_{3}\text{Li}$ has an excess of neutrons, it undergoes $\beta^{-}$ decay to form $^{8}_{4}\text{Be}$, emitting an electron ($e^{-}$) and an antineutrino ($\bar{\nu}$):

$^{8}_{3}\text{Li} \rightarrow ^{8}_{4}\text{Be} + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}$

The resulting $^{8}_{4}\text{Be}$ nucleus is highly unstable and immediately fissions into two $\alpha$-particles ($^{4}_{2}\text{He}$):

$^{8}_{4}\text{Be} \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

This sequence of reactions perfectly explains the ejection of electrons and $\alpha$-particles.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the maximum energy that a positron can possess during the $\beta^{+}$-decay of $^{11}\text{C}$ into $^{11}\text{B}$. The atomic masses of $^{11}\text{C}$ and $^{11}\text{B}$ are $11.0114 \text{ u}$ and $11.0093 \text{ u}$, respectively.
questions.solution:
The $\beta^{+}$ decay equation is given by:

$^{11}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{11}_{5}\text{B} + e^{+} + \nu_{e}$

The Q-value of the reaction is:

$Q = [m_{N}(^{11}\text{C}) - m_{N}(^{11}\text{B}) - m_e]c^2$

Expressing nuclear masses in terms of atomic masses:

$m_{N}(^{11}\text{C}) = m(^{11}\text{C}) - 6m_e$

$m_{N}(^{11}\text{B}) = m(^{11}\text{B}) - 5m_e$

Substituting these into the Q-value equation:

$Q = [m(^{11}\text{C}) - 6m_e - (m(^{11}\text{B}) - 5m_e) - m_e]c^2$

$Q = [m(^{11}\text{C}) - m(^{11}\text{B}) - 2m_e]c^2$

Given values:

$m(^{11}\text{C}) = 11.0114 \text{ u}$

$m(^{11}\text{B}) = 11.0093 \text{ u}$

$m_e = 0.0005486 \text{ u}$

Calculating the mass defect:

$\Delta m = 11.0114 - 11.0093 - 2(0.0005486)$

$\Delta m = 0.0021 - 0.0010972 = 0.0010028 \text{ u}$

Using the conversion factor $1 \text{ u} = 931 \text{ MeV}/c^2$:

$Q = 0.0010028 \times 931 \text{ MeV}$

$Q = 0.9336 \text{ MeV} = 933.6 \text{ keV}$

The maximum kinetic energy of the positron is equal to the Q-value of the reaction, which is $933.6 \text{ keV}$.

Answer: $933.6 \text{ keV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A $^{228}\text{Th}$ nucleus emits an alpha particle, reducing to $^{224}\text{Ra}$. Calculate the kinetic energy of the alpha particle emitted during the following decay:
$^{228}\text{Th} \to ^{224}\text{Ra}^{*} + \alpha$
$^{224}\text{Ra}^{*} \to ^{224}\text{Ra} + \gamma\;(217 \text{ keV})$.
The atomic mass of $^{228}\text{Th}$ is $228.028726 \text{ u}$, that of $^{224}\text{Ra}$ is $224.020196 \text{ u}$, and that of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ is $4.00260 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The mass defect for the decay to the ground state is given by:
$\Delta m = m(^{228}\text{Th}) - m(^{224}\text{Ra}) - m(^{4}_{2}\text{He})$
$\Delta m = 228.028726 - 224.020196 - 4.00260 = 0.005930 \text{ u}$

The total energy released (Q-value) in the decay to the ground state is:
$Q = \Delta m \times 931 \text{ MeV/u}$
$Q = 0.005930 \times 931 \approx 5.5208 \text{ MeV}$

Since the decay leaves the $^{224}\text{Ra}$ nucleus in an excited state which subsequently emits a $217 \text{ keV} = 0.217 \text{ MeV}$ gamma ray, the energy available for the kinetic energy of the alpha particle and the recoiling nucleus is:
$Q' = Q - E_{\gamma}$
$Q' = 5.5208 \text{ MeV} - 0.217 \text{ MeV} = 5.3038 \text{ MeV}$

By conservation of linear momentum, the kinetic energy of the emitted alpha particle is shared inversely with their masses:
$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{A - 4}{A} Q'$
where $A = 228$ is the mass number of the parent nucleus.

$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{224}{228} \times 5.3038 \text{ MeV}$
$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{56}{57} \times 5.3038 \text{ MeV} \approx 5.211 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the maximum kinetic energy of the beta particle emitted during the following decay scheme:
$^{12}\text{N} \to ^{12}\text{C}^{*} + e^{+} + \nu$
$^{12}\text{C}^{*} \to ^{12}\text{C} + \gamma\;(4.43 \text{ MeV})$.
The atomic mass of $^{12}\text{N}$ is given as $12.018613 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted positron ($e^{+}$) is equal to the $Q$-value of the decay process.

For a $\beta^{+}$ decay, the $Q$-value in terms of atomic masses is given by:
$Q = [m(^{12}\text{N}) - m(^{12}\text{C}^{*}) - 2m_e]c^2$

Since the $^{12}\text{C}^{*}$ nucleus is in an excited state and subsequently emits a gamma ray of energy $E_{\gamma} = 4.43 \text{ MeV}$ to reach the ground state, its mass can be written as:
$m(^{12}\text{C}^{*})c^2 = m(^{12}\text{C})c^2 + E_{\gamma}$

Substituting this into the $Q$-value equation, we get:
$K_{\max} = Q = [m(^{12}\text{N}) - m(^{12}\text{C})]c^2 - 2m_e c^2 - E_{\gamma}$

Given values:
Atomic mass of $^{12}\text{N} = 12.018613 \text{ u}$
Atomic mass of $^{12}\text{C} = 12.000000 \text{ u}$ (by definition)
Mass difference $\Delta m = 12.018613 - 12.000000 = 0.018613 \text{ u}$

Converting the mass difference into energy (using $1 \text{ u} \approx 931.5 \text{ MeV}/c^2$):
$\Delta m c^2 = 0.018613 \times 931.5 \text{ MeV} \approx 17.338 \text{ MeV}$

The rest mass energy of two electrons is:
$2m_e c^2 = 2 \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} = 1.022 \text{ MeV}$

Now, substituting the energies into the $K_{\max}$ equation:
$K_{\max} = 17.338 \text{ MeV} - 1.022 \text{ MeV} - 4.43 \text{ MeV}$

$K_{\max} = 11.886 \text{ MeV} \approx 11.88 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The decay constant of $^{197}_{80}\text{Hg}$ (which decays by electron capture to $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$) is $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$. What is the half-life of this isotope?
questions.solution:
The half-life $T_{1/2}$ of a radioactive isotope is related to its decay constant $\lambda$ by the formula:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

Given $\lambda = 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$ and using $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.8 \times 10^{-4}} \text{ s}$

$T_{1/2} = 3850 \text{ s}$

Converting the half-life from seconds to minutes:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{3850}{60} \text{ min}$

$T_{1/2} \approx 64.16 \text{ min} \approx 64.2 \text{ min}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The decay constant of $^{197}_{80}\text{Hg}$ (which decays by electron capture to $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$) is $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$. Determine the average-life of this isotope.
questions.solution:
The average life $\tau$ of a radioactive isotope is given by the reciprocal of its decay constant $\lambda$.

$\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$

Given $\lambda = 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$, substituting this value gives:

$\tau = \dfrac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{-4}} \text{ s} = \dfrac{10000}{1.8} \text{ s} = \dfrac{50000}{9} \text{ s}$

To convert the average life from seconds to minutes, divide by $60$:

$\tau = \dfrac{50000}{9 \times 60} \text{ min} = \dfrac{2500}{27} \text{ min}$

$\tau \approx 92.59 \text{ min} \approx 92.6 \text{ min}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The decay constant of $^{197}_{80}\text{Hg}$ (which decays by electron capture to $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$) is $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$. How much time is needed to convert $25\%$ of this mercury isotope into gold?
questions.solution:
Given that $25\%$ of the mercury isotope is converted into gold, the amount of mercury remaining is $75\%$ of the initial amount.

Let the initial amount be $N_0$. The remaining amount at time $t$ is $N = 0.75 N_0 = \dfrac{3}{4} N_0$.

Using the radioactive decay law:

$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

$\dfrac{3}{4} N_0 = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

$e^{\lambda t} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\lambda t = \ln\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) = \ln 4 - \ln 3$

Substituting the standard values $\ln 4 \approx 1.386$ and $\ln 3 \approx 1.098$:

$\lambda t \approx 1.386 - 1.098 = 0.288$

Given the decay constant $\lambda = 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$, the time $t$ is:

$t = \dfrac{0.288}{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}$

$t = 0.16 \times 10^4 \text{ s} = 1600 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Given that the half-life of $^{198}\text{Au}$ is $2.7 \text{ days}$, determine the activity of a sample which contains $1.00 \mu\text{g}$ of $^{198}\text{Au}$. Consider the atomic weight of $^{198}\text{Au}$ to be $198 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The number of atoms in the sample is given by:

$N = \dfrac{m}{M} \times N_A = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{-6}}{198} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.041 \times 10^{15} \text{ atoms}$

The decay constant is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{2.7 \times 24 \times 3600} \approx 2.97 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The activity of the sample is:

$A = \lambda N = (2.97 \times 10^{-6}) \times (3.041 \times 10^{15}) \approx 9.03 \times 10^9 \text{ Bq}$

Converting the activity to Curies ($1 \text{ Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10} \text{ Bq}$):

$A = \dfrac{9.03 \times 10^9}{3.7 \times 10^{10}} \approx 0.244 \text{ Ci}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the activity of a sample containing initially $1.00 \mu\text{g}$ of $^{198}\text{Au}$ after $7 \text{ days}$ have elapsed. The half-life of $^{198}\text{Au}$ is $2.7 \text{ days}$ and its atomic weight is $198 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The initial number of atoms $N_0$ in the sample is given by:

$N_0 = \dfrac{m}{M} \times N_A$

Substituting $m = 1.00 \mu\text{g} = 10^{-6} \text{ g}$, $M = 198 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, and $N_A = 6.023 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$:

$N_0 = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{198} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.04 \times 10^{15} \text{ atoms}$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{2.7 \times 24 \times 3600} \approx 2.97 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The initial activity $A_0$ is:

$A_0 = \lambda N_0 = (2.97 \times 10^{-6}) \times (3.04 \times 10^{15}) \approx 9.03 \times 10^9 \text{ decays/s}$

Converting this to Curies ($1 \text{ Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10} \text{ decays/s}$):

$A_0 = \dfrac{9.03 \times 10^9}{3.7 \times 10^{10}} \approx 0.244 \text{ Ci}$

The activity $A$ after $t = 7 \text{ days}$ is:

$A = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$

$A = 0.244 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{7}{2.7}}$

$A = 0.244 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2.59} \approx 0.244 \times 0.166 \approx 0.040 \text{ Ci}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample containing radioactive $^{131}\text{I}$ with a half-life of $8.0 \text{ days}$ has an initial activity of $20 \mu\text{Ci}$ at $t = 0$. Determine the activity of the sample at $t = 4.0 \text{ days}$.
questions.solution:
The activity of a radioactive sample at time $t$ is given by the formula:

$A(t) = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$

Given $A_0 = 20 \mu\text{Ci}$, $T_{1/2} = 8.0 \text{ days}$, and $t = 4.0 \text{ days}$.

Substituting the values:

$A(4.0) = 20 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{4.0}{8.0}}$

$A(4.0) = 20 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

$A(4.0) = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{2}}$

$A(4.0) = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 10 \times 1.414 = 14.14 \mu\text{Ci}$

The closest value is $14 \mu\text{Ci}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample containing radioactive $^{131}\text{I}$ with a half-life of $8.0 \text{ days}$ has an initial activity of $20 \mu\text{Ci}$ at $t = 0$. Find the decay constant of the sample at $t = 4.0 \text{ days}$.
questions.solution:
The decay constant $\lambda$ of a radioactive substance is a characteristic property of the nucleus and is independent of time and the amount of substance present.

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$

Given $T_{1/2} = 8.0 \text{ days} = 8.0 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 \text{ s} = 691200 \text{ s}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{691200} \text{ s}^{-1} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Given that the decay constant of $^{238}\text{U}$ is $4.9 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}$, find the half-life of $^{238}\text{U}$.
questions.solution:
The half-life of a radioactive substance is given by:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$

Substituting $\lambda = 4.9 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}$:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.9 \times 10^{-18}} \text{ s} = 1.414 \times 10^{17} \text{ s}$

Converting the half-life from seconds to years ($1 \text{ year} \approx 3.154 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$):

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{1.414 \times 10^{17}}{3.154 \times 10^7} \text{ y}$

$T_{1/2} \approx 4.48 \times 10^9 \text{ y} \approx 4.5 \times 10^9 \text{ y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The decay constant for $^{238}\text{U}$ is $4.9 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}$. Determine the average-life of $^{238}\text{U}$.
questions.solution:
The decay constant is given as $\lambda = 4.9 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

The average life $\tau$ is the reciprocal of the decay constant:

$\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{4.9 \times 10^{-18}} \text{ s} = 2.04 \times 10^{17} \text{ s}$

Converting seconds to years (using $1 \text{ year} \approx 3.14 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$):

$\tau = \dfrac{2.04 \times 10^{17}}{3.14 \times 10^7} \text{ y} \approx 6.49 \times 10^9 \text{ y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The decay constant of $^{238}\text{U}$ is $4.9 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}$. By what factor will the activity of a $^{238}\text{U}$ sample decrease in $9 \times 10^{9} \text{ years}$?
questions.solution:
The half-life of $^{238}\text{U}$ is given by:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.9 \times 10^{-18}} \text{ s} \approx 1.414 \times 10^{17} \text{ s}$

Converting the half-life into years (using $1 \text{ year} \approx 3.14 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$):

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{1.414 \times 10^{17}}{3.14 \times 10^7} \text{ years} \approx 4.5 \times 10^9 \text{ years}$

The given time is $t = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ years}$.

Number of half-lives, $n = \dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9}{4.5 \times 10^9} = 2$

The activity of the sample after $n$ half-lives is $A = \dfrac{A_0}{2^n}$.

Substituting $n = 2$:

$A = \dfrac{A_0}{2^2} = \dfrac{A_0}{4}$

Therefore, the activity decreases by a factor of $4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a certain time, a specific sample of a radioactive material decays at the rate of $500$ per second. After $50 \text{ minutes}$, the count rate falls to $200$ per second. Determine the decay constant of the sample.
questions.solution:
Given initial activity $A_0 = 500 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Activity after time $t = 50 \text{ minutes} = 3000 \text{ s}$ is $A = 200 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Using the radioactive decay law for activity, $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

Substituting the given values:

$200 = 500 e^{-\lambda \times 3000}$

$e^{3000 \lambda} = \dfrac{500}{200} = 2.5$

Taking natural logarithm on both sides:

$3000 \lambda = \ln(2.5)$

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.916}{3000}$

$\lambda = 3.05 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a certain time, a specific sample of a radioactive material decays at the rate of $500$ per second. After $50 \text{ minutes}$, the count rate falls to $200$ per second. Determine the half-life of the sample.
questions.solution:
The radioactive decay law is given by $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.

Given $A_0 = 500 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and $A = 200 \text{ s}^{-1}$ at $t = 50 \text{ min}$.

Substituting the values:

$200 = 500 e^{-50\lambda}$

$e^{50\lambda} = \dfrac{500}{200} = 2.5$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$50\lambda = \ln 2.5$

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2.5}{50}$

The half-life $T_{1/2}$ is given by:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{50 \ln 2}{\ln 2.5}$

Using $\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301$ and $\log_{10} 2.5 = \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{10}{4}\right) = 1 - 2\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.398$:

$T_{1/2} = 50 \times \dfrac{0.301}{0.398} \approx 37.8 \text{ min}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $38 \text{ min}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The half-life of $^{226}\text{Ra}$ is $1602 \text{ y}$. Determine the activity of $0.1 \text{ g}$ of $\text{RaCl}_2$, assuming all the radium present is in the form of $^{226}\text{Ra}$. Consider the atomic weight of $\text{Ra}$ to be $226 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and that of $\text{Cl}$ to be $35.5 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\text{RaCl}_2 = 226 + 2 \times 35.5 = 297 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $\text{RaCl}_2 = \dfrac{0.1}{297} \text{ mol}$

Since each molecule of $\text{RaCl}_2$ contains one atom of $\text{Ra}$, the number of $\text{Ra}$ atoms is:

$N = \dfrac{0.1}{297} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 2.028 \times 10^{20}$

The half-life of $^{226}\text{Ra}$ in seconds is:

$T_{1/2} = 1602 \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600 \text{ s} \approx 5.05 \times 10^{10} \text{ s}$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{5.05 \times 10^{10}} \approx 1.37 \times 10^{-11} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The activity $A$ of the sample is:

$A = \lambda N = 1.37 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.028 \times 10^{20} \approx 2.78 \times 10^9 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$

Rounding to the nearest given option, the activity is $2.8 \times 10^9 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Over a duration of $20 \text{ hours}$, the count rate from a radioactive sample drops from $4.0 \times 10^{6}$ per second to $1.0 \times 10^{6}$ per second. Calculate the count rate $100 \text{ hours}$ after the initial instant.
questions.solution:
The initial count rate is $R_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{6} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

After $t = 20 \text{ hours}$, the count rate is $R = 1.0 \times 10^{6} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Using the law of radioactive decay, $R = R_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$, where $n$ is the number of half-lives.

$1.0 \times 10^{6} = 4.0 \times 10^{6} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$

$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n} = \dfrac{1}{4} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow n = 2$

Since $2$ half-lives correspond to $20 \text{ hours}$, the half-life is $T_{1/2} = 10 \text{ hours}$.

For $t' = 100 \text{ hours}$, the number of half-lives is $n' = \dfrac{100}{10} = 10$.

The count rate after $100 \text{ hours}$ is $R' = R_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{10}$.

$R' = 4.0 \times 10^{6} \times \dfrac{1}{1024}$

$R' = \dfrac{4000 \times 10^{3}}{1024} \approx 3.9 \times 10^{3} \text{ per second}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioisotope has a half-life of $10 \text{ h}$. Determine the total number of disintegrations that occur in the tenth hour, measured from a time when the activity was $1 \text{ Ci}$.
questions.solution:
Initial activity $A_0 = 1 \text{ Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10} \text{ disintegrations/s}$.

Half-life $T_{1/2} = 10 \text{ h} = 36000 \text{ s}$.

Decay constant $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{10} \text{ h}^{-1}$.

The tenth hour corresponds to the time interval from $t = 9 \text{ h}$ to $t = 10 \text{ h}$. The total number of disintegrations $\Delta N$ in this interval is given by integrating the activity $A(t)$:

$\Delta N = \int_{9}^{10} A(t) dt = \int_{9}^{10} A_0 e^{-\lambda t} dt$

$\Delta N = \dfrac{A_0}{\lambda} \left( e^{-9\lambda} - e^{-10\lambda} \right)$

Since $e^{-\lambda t} = 2^{-t / T_{1/2}}$, we can rewrite this as:

$\Delta N = \dfrac{A_0 T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} \left( 2^{-9/10} - 2^{-10/10} \right)$

Substituting the values (with $T_{1/2}$ in seconds to match $A_0$):

$\dfrac{A_0 T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} = \dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{10} \times 36000}{0.693} \approx 1.922 \times 10^{15}$

Calculating the fractional part:

$2^{-0.9} - 2^{-1} \approx 0.5359 - 0.5000 = 0.0359$

Therefore, the total number of disintegrations is:

$\Delta N \approx 1.922 \times 10^{15} \times 0.0359 \approx 6.89 \times 10^{13}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $6.9 \times 10^{13}$.

Answer: $6.9 \times 10^{13}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The selling rate of a radioactive isotope is determined by its activity. What will be the second-hand rate of a one month old $^{32}\text{P}$ ($t_{1/2} = 14.3 \text{ days}$) source if it was initially purchased for $800$ rupees? (Assume $1 \text{ month} = 30 \text{ days}$)
questions.solution:
The selling rate of the radioactive isotope is directly proportional to its activity.

The activity of a radioactive sample after time $t$ is given by $A = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{t_{1/2}}}$.

Since the price is proportional to the activity, the new price $P$ after time $t$ is $P = P_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{t_{1/2}}}$.

Given $P_0 = 800 \text{ rupees}$, $t = 30 \text{ days}$, and $t_{1/2} = 14.3 \text{ days}$.

Substituting the values:

$P = 800 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{30}{14.3}}$

$P = 800 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2.098}$

$P = \dfrac{800}{2^{2.098}} \approx \dfrac{800}{4.28} \approx 187 \text{ rupees}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: By $\beta^{+}$-emission, $^{57}\text{Co}$ decays into $^{57}\text{Fe}$. The produced $^{57}\text{Fe}$ is initially in an excited state and transitions to the ground state by emitting $\gamma$-rays. The half-life for the $\beta^{+}$-decay is $270 \text{ days}$, while the half-life for the $\gamma$-emission is $10^{-8} \text{ s}$. If a $^{57}\text{Co}$ sample currently emits $5.0 \times 10^{9}$ gamma rays per second, what time will elapse until the gamma ray emission rate drops to $2.5 \times 10^{9}$ per second?
questions.solution:
The decay sequence is $^{57}\text{Co} \xrightarrow{\beta^+} {}^{57}\text{Fe}^{*} \xrightarrow{\gamma} {}^{57}\text{Fe}$.

Since the half-life of $^{57}\text{Co}$ ($270 \text{ days}$) is much greater than the half-life of the excited $^{57}\text{Fe}^{*}$ state ($10^{-8} \text{ s}$), secular equilibrium is established almost instantaneously.

In secular equilibrium, the rate of formation of the daughter nucleus is equal to its rate of decay. Thus, the activity of $^{57}\text{Fe}^{*}$ ($\gamma$-emission rate) is equal to the activity of $^{57}\text{Co}$ ($\beta^{+}$-emission rate).

The $\gamma$-emission rate will therefore decay with the half-life of the parent $^{57}\text{Co}$ nucleus.

The $\gamma$-emission rate drops from $5.0 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$ to $2.5 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$, which is exactly half of its initial value.

The time required for the activity to become half is one half-life of $^{57}\text{Co}$, which is $270 \text{ days}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Carbon ($Z = 6$) possessing mass number $11$ decays into boron ($Z = 5$). Identify the type of decay taking place.
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction for the decay of Carbon-11 into Boron-11 can be written as:

$^{11}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{11}_{5}\text{B} + ^{0}_{+1}e + \nu$

In this process, the mass number remains unchanged ($A = 11$) while the atomic number decreases by $1$ (from $Z = 6$ to $Z = 5$). This indicates that a proton is converted into a neutron, emitting a positron ($e^{+}$ or $\beta^{+}$) and a neutrino ($\nu$).

Therefore, the process is $\beta^{+}$-decay.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Carbon ($Z = 6$) possessing mass number $11$ decays into boron ($Z = 5$). The half-life for this decay scheme is $20.3 \text{ minutes}$. Calculate the time elapsed before a mixture containing $90\%$ carbon-11 and $10\%$ boron-11 (by number of atoms) transforms into a mixture of $10\%$ carbon-11 and $90\%$ boron-11.
questions.solution:
Let the total number of atoms in the mixture be $N$.

Initially, the number of Carbon-11 atoms is $N_1 = 0.90 N$.

Finally, the number of Carbon-11 atoms is $N_2 = 0.10 N$.

According to the law of radioactive decay:

$N_2 = N_1 e^{-\lambda t}$

$0.10 N = 0.90 N e^{-\lambda t}$

$e^{\lambda t} = 9$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\lambda t = \ln 9 = 2 \ln 3$

Since the decay constant $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$, we get:

$t = \dfrac{2 \ln 3}{\ln 2} T_{1/2}$

Substituting $T_{1/2} = 20.3 \text{ minutes}$:

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 0.4771}{0.3010} \times 20.3$

$t \approx 3.17 \times 20.3 \approx 64.35 \text{ minutes}$

The closest value is $64.3 \text{ minutes}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel contains $4 \times 10^{23}$ tritium atoms. Given that the half-life for the decay of tritium nuclei is $12.3 \text{ y}$, determine the activity of the sample.
questions.solution:
The activity of a radioactive sample is given by the formula:

$A = \lambda N$

where $\lambda$ is the decay constant and $N$ is the number of atoms.

The decay constant $\lambda$ is related to the half-life $T_{1/2}$ by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} \approx \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}}$

Given:

$T_{1/2} = 12.3 \text{ y} = 12.3 \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600 \text{ s} = 3.879 \times 10^8 \text{ s}$

$N = 4 \times 10^{23}$

Substituting these values into the activity formula:

$A = \dfrac{0.693}{3.879 \times 10^8} \times 4 \times 10^{23}$

$A \approx 1.786 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^{23}$

$A \approx 7.146 \times 10^{14} \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel holds $4 \times 10^{23}$ tritium atoms. If the half-life for the decay of tritium nuclei is $12.3 \text{ y}$, calculate the number of decays taking place in the subsequent $10 \text{ hours}$.
questions.solution:
The number of decays in a small time interval $t$ is given by $\Delta N = \lambda N_0 t$, since $t \ll T_{1/2}$.

The decay constant $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$.

Given $T_{1/2} = 12.3 \text{ y} = 12.3 \times 365 \times 24 \text{ hours} = 107748 \text{ hours}$.

Substituting the values:

$\Delta N = \dfrac{0.693}{107748} \times 4 \times 10^{23} \times 10$

$\Delta N \approx 2.57 \times 10^{19}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Inside a vessel, there are $4 \times 10^{23}$ tritium atoms. The half-life for the decay of tritium nuclei is $12.3 \text{ y}$. Evaluate the number of decays that will occur over the next $6.15 \text{ y}$.
questions.solution:
The number of remaining atoms after time $t$ is given by the radioactive decay law:

$N = N_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$

Given $N_0 = 4 \times 10^{23}$, $T_{1/2} = 12.3 \text{ y}$, and $t = 6.15 \text{ y}$.

The number of half-lives elapsed is $n = \dfrac{6.15}{12.3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Substituting the values:

$N = 4 \times 10^{23} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{23}}{\sqrt{2}}$

The number of decays that occur is the difference between the initial number of atoms and the remaining atoms:

$\Delta N = N_0 - N = 4 \times 10^{23} - \dfrac{4 \times 10^{23}}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\Delta N = 4 \times 10^{23} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

Using $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$\Delta N = 4 \times 10^{23} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.414}\right) \approx 4 \times 10^{23} (1 - 0.707)$

$\Delta N = 4 \times 10^{23} \times 0.293 = 1.172 \times 10^{23}$

The number of decays is approximately $1.17 \times 10^{23}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point source emitting alpha particles is situated at a distance of $1 \text{ m}$ from a counter that registers any alpha particle striking its $1 \text{ cm}^2$ window. Given that the source has $6.0 \times 10^{16}$ active nuclei and the counter registers a rate of $50000 \text{ counts/second}$, determine the decay constant. Assume the source radiates alpha particles uniformly in all directions and that the alpha particles strike the window nearly normally.
questions.solution:
The total activity of the source is given by $A_0 = \lambda N$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant and $N$ is the number of active nuclei.

Since the alpha particles are emitted uniformly in all directions, the fraction of particles hitting the window is the ratio of the area of the window to the total surface area of a sphere of radius $r$.

Fraction of particles registered $= \dfrac{A}{4\pi r^2}$

The count rate $C$ is the number of alpha particles striking the window per second:

$C = A_0 \times \dfrac{A}{4\pi r^2} = \lambda N \dfrac{A}{4\pi r^2}$

Rearranging for the decay constant $\lambda$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{C \times 4\pi r^2}{N \times A}$

Substituting the given values $C = 50000 \text{ s}^{-1}$, $r = 1 \text{ m} = 100 \text{ cm}$, $A = 1 \text{ cm}^2$, and $N = 6.0 \times 10^{16}$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{50000 \times 4\pi \times (100)^2}{6.0 \times 10^{16} \times 1}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{5 \times 10^4 \times 4\pi \times 10^4}{6.0 \times 10^{16}}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{20\pi \times 10^8}{6.0 \times 10^{16}}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{10\pi}{3} \times 10^{-8} \text{ s}^{-1}$

$\lambda \approx 10.47 \times 10^{-8} \text{ s}^{-1} = 1.047 \times 10^{-7} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Rounding to three significant figures, we get $1.05 \times 10^{-7} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Charcoal prepared from a living tree exhibits a disintegration rate of $15.3$ disintegrations of $^{14}\text{C}$ per gram per minute. An ancient charcoal sample has a $^{14}\text{C}$ activity of $12.3$ disintegrations per gram per minute. Determine the age of this sample given that the half-life of $^{14}\text{C}$ is $5730 \text{ y}$.
questions.solution:
The radioactive decay law is given by:

$t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda} \log \left( \dfrac{A_0}{A} \right)$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{5730} \text{ y}^{-1}$

Given:

$A_0 = 15.3 \text{ dis min}^{-1} \text{ g}^{-1}$

$A = 12.3 \text{ dis min}^{-1} \text{ g}^{-1}$

Substituting the values into the decay equation:

$t = \dfrac{2.303 \times 5730}{0.693} \log \left( \dfrac{15.3}{12.3} \right)$

$t = \dfrac{13196.19}{0.693} \log (1.2439)$

$t = 19042.1 \times 0.0948$

$t \approx 1805 \text{ y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Natural water contains a trace amount of tritium ($^{3}_{1}\text{H}$). This isotope beta-decays with a half-life of $12.5 \text{ years}$. While ascending a difficult peak, a mountaineer discovers debris from a previous unsuccessful attempt, which includes a sealed bottle of whisky. Upon returning, the mountaineer analyses the whisky and determines that it contains merely $1.5\%$ of the $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$ radioactivity compared to a recently purchased bottle marked '8 years old'. Estimate the time that has elapsed since that unsuccessful attempt.
questions.solution:
Let the initial radioactivity of the natural water used to make the whisky be $A_0$.

For the recently purchased bottle marked '8 years old', the water was drawn 8 years ago. Its present radioactivity is:
$A_1 = A_0 e^{-8\lambda}$

Assuming the found bottle was also an '8 years old' whisky when it was left on the peak $t$ years ago, the total time elapsed since its water was drawn is $(t + 8)$ years. Its present radioactivity is:
$A_2 = A_0 e^{-(t+8)\lambda}$

Given that the found bottle contains $1.5\%$ of the radioactivity of the recently purchased bottle:
$A_2 = 0.015 A_1$

Substituting the expressions for $A_1$ and $A_2$:
$A_0 e^{-(t+8)\lambda} = 0.015 A_0 e^{-8\lambda}$

Dividing both sides by $A_0 e^{-8\lambda}$:
$e^{-\lambda t} = 0.015$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:
$-\lambda t = \ln(0.015)$

Using the decay constant formula $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$:
$t = \dfrac{-\ln(0.015)}{\ln 2} \times T_{1/2}$

$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\dfrac{1000}{15}\right)}{\ln 2} \times 12.5$

$t = \dfrac{\ln(66.67)}{\ln 2} \times 12.5$

$t \approx 6.059 \times 12.5 \approx 75.7 \text{ years}$

The time elapsed since the unsuccessful attempt is approximately $75.7 \text{ years}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $^{238}\text{U}$ decays to $^{206}\text{Pb}$ with a half-life of $4.47 \times 10^{9} \text{ y}$ through a chain of processes. A rock sample is discovered to contain $2.00 \text{ mg}$ of $^{238}\text{U}$ and $0.600 \text{ mg}$ of $^{206}\text{Pb}$. Assuming that all the lead originated from the uranium, determine the life of the rock.
questions.solution:
Let $N$ be the present number of $^{238}\text{U}$ atoms and $N_{Pb}$ be the present number of $^{206}\text{Pb}$ atoms.

The number of moles of $^{238}\text{U}$ is $n_U = \dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{238}$

The number of moles of $^{206}\text{Pb}$ is $n_{Pb} = \dfrac{0.600 \times 10^{-3}}{206}$

Since all the lead originated from the uranium, the initial number of moles of $^{238}\text{U}$ was:

$n_0 = n_U + n_{Pb}$

The ratio of the initial amount of uranium to the present amount is:

$\dfrac{n_0}{n_U} = 1 + \dfrac{n_{Pb}}{n_U} = 1 + \dfrac{\dfrac{0.600}{206}}{\dfrac{2.00}{238}}$

$\dfrac{n_0}{n_U} = 1 + \dfrac{0.600 \times 238}{2.00 \times 206} = 1 + \dfrac{142.8}{412} = 1 + 0.3466 = 1.3466$

According to the radioactive decay law, $n_U = n_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, which gives:

$t = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} \ln\left(\dfrac{n_0}{n_U}\right) = \dfrac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} \ln\left(\dfrac{n_0}{n_U}\right)$

Substituting the given values:

$t = \dfrac{4.47 \times 10^{9}}{0.693} \ln(1.3466)$

$t = \dfrac{4.47 \times 10^{9}}{0.693} \times 0.2976 \approx 1.919 \times 10^{9} \text{ y}$

Rounding to three significant figures, the life of the rock is $1.92 \times 10^{9} \text{ y}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The count rate of nuclear radiation emitted from a radioactive sample containing $^{128}\text{I}$ varies with time in the following manner.
Time $t$ (minute)$0$$25$$50$$75$$100$
Count rate $R$ ($10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$)$30$$16$$8.0$$3.8$$2.0$

Determine the decay constant $\lambda$ from the slope of the best straight line through the points.
questions.solution:
The radioactive decay equation is given by:

$R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\ln R = \ln R_0 - \lambda t$

This represents the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, where $y = \ln R$, $x = t$, and the slope is $m = -\lambda$.

Using the data points at $t_1 = 25 \text{ min}$ and $t_2 = 100 \text{ min}$:

$R_1 = 16 \times 10^9 \text{ s}^{-1}$

$R_2 = 2.0 \times 10^9 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The slope $m$ is given by:

$m = \dfrac{\ln R_2 - \ln R_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \dfrac{\ln(2.0) - \ln(16)}{100 - 25}$

$m = \dfrac{\ln\left(\dfrac{2.0}{16}\right)}{75} = \dfrac{\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)}{75} = \dfrac{-3 \ln 2}{75} = \dfrac{-\ln 2}{25}$

Since $\lambda = -m$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{25} \approx \dfrac{0.693}{25} = 0.0277 \text{ min}^{-1} \approx 0.028 \text{ min}^{-1}$

This is consistent with the other data points, confirming the decay constant is approximately $0.028 \text{ min}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
For a radioactive sample containing $^{128}\text{I}$, let $R_0$ be the initial count rate and $R$ be the count rate of the nuclear radiation at time $t$. What is the nature of the plot of $\ln(R_0/R)$ against $t$?
Time $t$ (minute)$0$$25$$50$$75$$100$
Count rate $R$ ($10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$)$30$$16$$8.0$$3.8$$2.0$
options: A parabola passing through the origin
A straight line passing through the origin
A straight line with a non-zero y-intercept
questions.solution:
According to the law of radioactive decay, the count rate $R$ at time $t$ is given by:

$R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

where $R_0$ is the initial count rate and $\lambda$ is the decay constant.

Rearranging the equation, we get:

$\dfrac{R_0}{R} = e^{\lambda t}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{R_0}{R}\right) = \lambda t$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, we have $y = \ln(R_0/R)$, $x = t$, $m = \lambda$, and $c = 0$.

Thus, the plot of $\ln(R_0/R)$ against $t$ is a straight line passing through the origin.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The decay constant $\lambda$ for a radioactive sample containing $^{128}\text{I}$ is found to be approximately $0.028 \text{ min}^{-1}$. Calculate the half-life $t_{1/2}$.
Time $t$ (minute)$0$$25$$50$$75$$100$
Count rate $R$ ($10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$)$30$$16$$8.0$$3.8$$2.0$
questions.solution:
The relation between half-life $t_{1/2}$ and decay constant $\lambda$ is given by:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

Substituting $\lambda = 0.028 \text{ min}^{-1}$:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.028} = 24.75 \text{ min} \approx 25 \text{ min}$

Alternatively, observing the given table, the count rate $R$ becomes approximately half of its value after every $25 \text{ min}$. For instance, at $t = 25 \text{ min}$, $R = 16 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$ which is roughly half of the initial value $30 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$. At $t = 50 \text{ min}$, $R = 8.0 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$ which is exactly half of $16 \times 10^{9} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Thus, the half-life is $25 \text{ min}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The half-life of $^{40}\text{K}$ is $1.30 \times 10^{9} \text{ y}$. A $1.00 \text{ g}$ sample of pure $\text{KCl}$ yields $160 \text{ counts s}^{-1}$. Determine the relative abundance of $^{40}\text{K}$ (the fraction of $^{40}\text{K}$ present) in natural potassium.
questions.solution:
The decay constant $\lambda$ of $^{40}\text{K}$ is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.30 \times 10^{9} \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600 \text{ s}} = 1.69 \times 10^{-17} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The activity $A$ is $160 \text{ counts s}^{-1}$. The number of $^{40}\text{K}$ atoms in the sample is:

$N_{40} = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{160}{1.69 \times 10^{-17}} = 9.47 \times 10^{18} \text{ atoms}$

The molar mass of $\text{KCl}$ is approximately $39.1 + 35.5 = 74.6 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$. The total number of potassium atoms in $1.00 \text{ g}$ of $\text{KCl}$ is:

$N_{\text{K}} = \dfrac{1.00}{74.6} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 8.07 \times 10^{21} \text{ atoms}$

The relative abundance of $^{40}\text{K}$ in natural potassium is the ratio of the number of $^{40}\text{K}$ atoms to the total number of $\text{K}$ atoms:

$\text{Relative abundance} = \dfrac{N_{40}}{N_{\text{K}}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{9.47 \times 10^{18}}{8.07 \times 10^{21}} \times 100\% = 0.117\%$

Rounding off, we get $0.12\%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $^{197}_{80}\text{Hg}$ decays to $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$ via electron capture, with a decay constant of $0.257$ per day. Determine the other particle or particles that are emitted in this decay.
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction for the electron capture process is given by:

$^{197}_{80}\text{Hg} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \rightarrow ^{197}_{79}\text{Au} + \nu_{e}$

In an electron capture process, a proton in the nucleus captures an inner-shell electron and converts into a neutron. To conserve the lepton number, an electron neutrino ($\nu_{e}$) is emitted.

Thus, the other particle emitted in this decay is a neutrino.

Assuming the captured electron comes from the $K$ shell, determine the wavelength of the $K_\alpha$ X-ray emitted subsequent to the electron capture. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment, a radioactive isotope is produced at a constant rate $dN/dt = R$. The isotope has a half-life $t_{1/2}$. After a time $t \gg t_{1/2}$, the number of active nuclei becomes constant. Determine the value of this constant.
questions.solution:
The rate of change of the number of active nuclei is given by the difference between the rate of production and the rate of decay.

$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = R - \lambda N$

where $R$ is the constant production rate and $\lambda$ is the decay constant.

After a long time ($t \gg t_{1/2}$), the number of active nuclei becomes constant, which means the system reaches a steady state.

At steady state, $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 0$

$R - \lambda N = 0 \Rightarrow N = \dfrac{R}{\lambda}$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is related to the half-life $t_{1/2}$ by the equation:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$

Substituting the value of $\lambda$ into the expression for $N$:

$N = \dfrac{R}{\left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}\right)} = \dfrac{R t_{1/2}}{\ln 2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment, a radioactive isotope is generated at a constant rate $dN/dt = R$. The isotope has a half-life $t_{1/2}$. Assuming that the generation of the radioactive isotope begins at $t = 0$, determine the number of active nuclei at time $t$.
questions.solution:
The rate of change of the number of active nuclei is the difference between the rate of generation and the rate of decay.

$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = R - \lambda N$

where $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$ is the decay constant.

Rearranging the variables:

$\dfrac{dN}{R - \lambda N} = dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ to $t$, with $N(0) = 0$:

$\int_{0}^{N} \dfrac{dN}{R - \lambda N} = \int_{0}^{t} dt$

$-\dfrac{1}{\lambda} [\ln(R - \lambda N)]_{0}^{N} = t$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{R - \lambda N}{R}\right) = -\lambda t$

$\dfrac{R - \lambda N}{R} = e^{-\lambda t}$

$R - \lambda N = R e^{-\lambda t}$

$N = \dfrac{R}{\lambda} \left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: During an agricultural experiment, a solution containing $1\text{ mole}$ of a radioactive material ($t_{1/2} = 14.3\text{ days}$) was injected into the roots of a plant. The plant was left to settle for $70\text{ hours}$, after which the activity in its fruit was measured. If the measured activity was $1\mu\text{Ci}$, what percentage of the activity is transmitted from the root to the fruit in steady state?
questions.solution:
The initial number of radioactive atoms in $1\text{ mole}$ is:

$N_0 = 6.023 \times 10^{23}$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{14.3 \times 24 \times 3600} = 5.61 \times 10^{-7}\text{ s}^{-1}$

The initial activity $A_0$ of the injected material is:

$A_0 = \lambda N_0 = (5.61 \times 10^{-7}) \times (6.023 \times 10^{23}) = 3.38 \times 10^{17}\text{ Bq}$

The plant is left to settle for $t = 70\text{ hours} = \dfrac{70}{24}\text{ days} = 2.92\text{ days}$. The total activity of the radioactive material remaining in the plant after this time is:

$A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t} = A_0 e^{-\dfrac{0.693 \times 2.92}{14.3}}$

$A(t) = 3.38 \times 10^{17} \times e^{-0.141} \approx 3.38 \times 10^{17} \times 0.868 = 2.93 \times 10^{17}\text{ Bq}$

The measured activity in the fruit is:

$A_f = 1\mu\text{Ci} = 10^{-6} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq} = 3.7 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$

In steady state, the percentage of activity transmitted from the root to the fruit is the ratio of the activity in the fruit to the total remaining activity in the plant:

$\text{Percentage transmitted} = \dfrac{A_f}{A(t)} \times 100$

$\text{Percentage transmitted} = \dfrac{3.7 \times 10^4}{2.93 \times 10^{17}} \times 100 = 1.26 \times 10^{-13} \times 100 = 1.26 \times 10^{-11} \%$

Answer: $1.26 \times 10^{-11} \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel with a volume of $125 \text{ cm}^3$ holds tritium ($^{3}\text{H}$, $t_{1/2} = 12.3 \text{ y}$) gas at a pressure of $500 \text{ kPa}$ and a temperature of $300 \text{ K}$. Determine the activity of the gas.
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, the number of moles of tritium gas is:

$n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{500 \times 10^3 \times 125 \times 10^{-6}}{8.314 \times 300} \approx 0.025 \text{ mol}$

Since tritium gas ($^{3}\text{H}_2$) is diatomic, the total number of radioactive tritium atoms is:

$N = 2nN_A = 2 \times 0.025 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.01 \times 10^{22}$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{12.3 \times 365.25 \times 24 \times 3600} \approx 1.786 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The activity $A$ of the gas is:

$A = \lambda N = (1.786 \times 10^{-9}) \times (3.01 \times 10^{22}) \approx 5.38 \times 10^{13} \text{ Bq}$

Converting the activity to Curies ($1 \text{ Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10} \text{ Bq}$):

$A = \dfrac{5.38 \times 10^{13}}{3.7 \times 10^{10}} \approx 1454 \text{ Ci}$

The closest value among the given options is $1448 \text{ Ci}$.

Answer: $1448 \text{ Ci}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The nuclide $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is capable of disintegrating by emitting either an $\alpha$-particle or a $\beta^{-}$-particle. Identify the correct pair of equations showing the products of these two decay modes.
questions.solution:
In $\alpha$-decay, the parent nucleus emits an $\alpha$-particle ($^{4}_{2}\text{He}$). The mass number decreases by $4$ and the atomic number decreases by $2$.

$^{212}_{83}\text{Bi} \rightarrow ^{208}_{81}\text{Tl} + \alpha$

In $\beta^{-}$-decay, the parent nucleus emits an electron ($e^{-}$) and an antineutrino ($\bar{\nu}$). The mass number remains unchanged and the atomic number increases by $1$.

$^{212}_{83}\text{Bi} \rightarrow ^{212}_{84}\text{Po} + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The nuclide $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is capable of disintegrating by emitting either an $\alpha$-particle or a $\beta^{-}$-particle. The probabilities for disintegration via $\alpha$- and $\beta$-decays stand in the ratio $7/13$. The overall half-life of $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is one hour. Suppose $1 \text{ g}$ of pure $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is taken at $12.00$ noon. Determine the composition of this sample at $1$ p.m. on the same day.
options: $0.50 \text{ g}$ Bi, $0.325 \text{ g}$ Tl, $0.175 \text{ g}$ Po
$0.50 \text{ g}$ Bi, $0.175 \text{ g}$ Tl, $0.325 \text{ g}$ Po
$0.50 \text{ g}$ Bi, $0.25 \text{ g}$ Tl, $0.25 \text{ g}$ Po
questions.solution:
The initial mass of $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is $1 \text{ g}$.

The overall half-life of $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ is $1 \text{ hour}$. Since the time elapsed from $12.00$ noon to $1$ p.m. is exactly $1 \text{ hour}$ (one half-life), the amount of $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ remaining is:

$W_{\text{Bi}} = 1 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^1 = 0.50 \text{ g}$

The mass of $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ that has decayed is:

$W_{\text{decayed}} = 1 - 0.50 = 0.50 \text{ g}$

The decay occurs via two parallel pathways:
$\alpha$-decay: $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi} \rightarrow ^{208}_{81}\text{Tl} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$
$\beta$-decay: $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi} \rightarrow ^{212}_{84}\text{Po} + \beta^{-}$

The probabilities for $\alpha$- and $\beta$-decays are in the ratio $7/13$. Therefore, the fractions of the decayed $^{212}_{83}\text{Bi}$ that undergo $\alpha$- and $\beta$-decay are $\dfrac{7}{20}$ and $\dfrac{13}{20}$, respectively.

Assuming the mass of the products is approximately equal to the mass of the decayed parent nuclei (as indicated by the options), we get:

Mass of Tl formed $= 0.50 \times \dfrac{7}{20} = 0.175 \text{ g}$

Mass of Po formed $= 0.50 \times \dfrac{13}{20} = 0.325 \text{ g}$

The composition of the sample at $1$ p.m. is $0.50 \text{ g}$ Bi, $0.175 \text{ g}$ Tl, and $0.325 \text{ g}$ Po.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A sample contains a mixture of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ isotopes, each having an initial activity of $8.0 \times 10^{8}$ disintegrations per second. $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is known to have a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$. The total activity $A$ is measured as a function of time, and the following data are obtained.
Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)
$20$$11.799$$200$$3.0828$
$40$$9.1680$$300$$1.8899$
$60$$7.4492$$400$$1.1671$
$80$$6.2684$$500$$0.7212$
$100$$5.4115$

If a plot of $\ln(A/A_0)$ versus time is constructed (where $A_0$ is the total initial activity), what is the expected shape of the curve?
options: A curve that starts with a steeper negative slope and asymptotically approaches a straight line with a less steep negative slope.
A straight line with a constant negative slope.
A curve that starts with a less steep negative slope and asymptotically approaches a straight line with a steeper negative slope.
questions.solution:
The total activity $A(t)$ of the mixture is the sum of the activities of the two isotopes:

$A(t) = A_{01} e^{-\lambda_1 t} + A_{02} e^{-\lambda_2 t}$

Given that the initial activities are equal, $A_{01} = A_{02} = \dfrac{A_0}{2}$, where $A_0$ is the total initial activity.

$A(t) = \dfrac{A_0}{2} (e^{-\lambda_1 t} + e^{-\lambda_2 t})$

$\dfrac{A(t)}{A_0} = \dfrac{1}{2} (e^{-\lambda_1 t} + e^{-\lambda_2 t})$

Taking the natural logarithm:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{A}{A_0}\right) = \ln\left(e^{-\lambda_1 t} + e^{-\lambda_2 t}\right) - \ln 2$

The slope of the curve is given by the derivative with respect to time:

$\text{Slope} = \dfrac{d}{dt} \ln\left(\dfrac{A}{A_0}\right) = \dfrac{-\lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_1 t} - \lambda_2 e^{-\lambda_2 t}}{e^{-\lambda_1 t} + e^{-\lambda_2 t}}$

At $t = 0$, the initial slope is:

$m_{\text{initial}} = -\dfrac{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}{2}$

Since $^{108}\text{Ag}$ has a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$, its decay constant is smaller, so $\lambda_2 < \lambda_1$.

As $t \to \infty$, the term with the larger decay constant ($e^{-\lambda_1 t}$) approaches zero much faster than $e^{-\lambda_2 t}$. The slope asymptotically approaches:

$m_{\text{final}} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \dfrac{-\lambda_1 e^{-(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2) t} - \lambda_2}{e^{-(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2) t} + 1} = -\lambda_2$

Comparing the magnitudes of the slopes:

$|m_{\text{initial}}| = \dfrac{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}{2} > \lambda_2 = |m_{\text{final}}|$

The initial slope is more negative (steeper) than the final slope. Therefore, the curve starts with a steeper negative slope and asymptotically approaches a straight line with a less steep negative slope.

questions.q:
A sample contains a mixture of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ isotopes, each having an initial activity of $8.0 \times 10^{8}$ disintegrations per second. $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is known to have a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$. The total activity $A$ is measured as a function of time. For large values of time, the plot of $\ln(A/A_0)$ versus time is nearly linear. Deduce the half-life of $^{108}\text{Ag}$ from this portion of the plot.
Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)
$20$$11.799$$200$$3.0828$
$40$$9.1680$$300$$1.8899$
$60$$7.4492$$400$$1.1671$
$80$$6.2684$$500$$0.7212$
$100$$5.4115$
questions.solution:
The total activity of the mixture is given by $A = A_{10} e^{-\lambda_1 t} + A_{20} e^{-\lambda_2 t}$, where $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the decay constants of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ respectively.

Since $^{108}\text{Ag}$ has a larger half-life, its decay constant $\lambda_2$ is smaller than $\lambda_1$. For large values of time $t$, the term $e^{-\lambda_1 t}$ decays much faster and becomes negligible compared to $e^{-\lambda_2 t}$.

Thus, for large $t$, the total activity is approximately $A \approx A_{20} e^{-\lambda_2 t}$.

Using the data for large times, at $t_1 = 400 \text{ s}$, $A_1 = 1.1671 \times 10^8 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and at $t_2 = 500 \text{ s}$, $A_2 = 0.7212 \times 10^8 \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Taking the ratio of the activities:

$\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda_2 t_1}}{e^{-\lambda_2 t_2}} = e^{\lambda_2 (t_2 - t_1)}$

$\dfrac{1.1671}{0.7212} = e^{\lambda_2 (500 - 400)}$

$1.618 = e^{100 \lambda_2}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$100 \lambda_2 = \ln(1.618) \approx 0.481$

$\lambda_2 = 0.00481 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The half-life of $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.00481} \approx 144 \text{ s}$

questions.q:
A sample contains a mixture of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ isotopes, each having an initial activity of $8.0 \times 10^{8}$ disintegrations per second. $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is known to have a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$, specifically $144 \text{ s}$. Calculate the activity corresponding to $^{110}\text{Ag}$ at $t = 50 \text{ s}$.
Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)
$20$$11.799$$200$$3.0828$
$40$$9.1680$$300$$1.8899$
$60$$7.4492$$400$$1.1671$
$80$$6.2684$$500$$0.7212$
$100$$5.4115$
questions.solution:
The total activity of the sample at any time $t$ is the sum of the activities of the two isotopes:

$A(t) = A_{110}(t) + A_{108}(t)$

For $^{108}\text{Ag}$, the initial activity is $A_{108}(0) = 8.0 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$ and its half-life is $T_{1/2} = 144 \text{ s}$. The activity of $^{108}\text{Ag}$ at $t = 100 \text{ s}$ is:

$A_{108}(100) = 8.0 \times 10^8 \times e^{-\dfrac{100 \ln 2}{144}} = 8.0 \times 10^8 \times e^{-0.4813} \approx 4.943 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$

From the given table, the total activity at $t = 100 \text{ s}$ is $A(100) = 5.4115 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$. Thus, the activity of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ at $t = 100 \text{ s}$ is:

$A_{110}(100) = A(100) - A_{108}(100) = (5.4115 - 4.943) \times 10^8 = 0.4685 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$

Since radioactive decay follows an exponential law ($A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$), the activity at the midpoint $t = 50 \text{ s}$ is the geometric mean of the activities at $t = 0 \text{ s}$ and $t = 100 \text{ s}$:

$A_{110}(50) = \sqrt{A_{110}(0) \times A_{110}(100)}$

$A_{110}(50) = \sqrt{8.0 \times 10^8 \times 0.4685 \times 10^8} = \sqrt{3.748} \times 10^8 \approx 1.93 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations s}^{-1}$

This is closest to $1.9 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations per second}$.

Answer: $1.9 \times 10^8 \text{ disintegrations per second}$

questions.q:
A sample contains a mixture of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ isotopes, each having an initial activity of $8.0 \times 10^{8}$ disintegrations per second. $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is known to have a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$. If one plots $\ln(A_{110}/A_{0,110})$ versus time for $^{110}\text{Ag}$ for the first $50 \text{ s}$, what is the expected shape of the plot?
Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)
$20$$11.799$$200$$3.0828$
$40$$9.1680$$300$$1.8899$
$60$$7.4492$$400$$1.1671$
$80$$6.2684$$500$$0.7212$
$100$$5.4115$
options: A straight line with a positive slope.
A straight line with a negative slope.
A curve with a decreasingly negative slope.
A curve with an increasingly negative slope.
questions.solution:
The activity of a single radioactive isotope follows the exponential decay law:

$A_{110} = A_{0,110} e^{-\lambda_{110} t}$

where $A_{110}$ is the activity at time $t$, $A_{0,110}$ is the initial activity, and $\lambda_{110}$ is the decay constant of $^{110}\text{Ag}$.

Dividing by $A_{0,110}$ and taking the natural logarithm on both sides, we get:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{A_{110}}{A_{0,110}}\right) = -\lambda_{110} t$

This equation represents a linear relationship of the form $y = mx$, where the y-axis is $\ln\left(\dfrac{A_{110}}{A_{0,110}}\right)$ and the x-axis is time $t$.

The slope of this line is $m = -\lambda_{110}$. Since the decay constant $\lambda_{110}$ is a positive quantity, the slope is negative.

Thus, the expected shape of the plot is a straight line with a negative slope. The provided table of total activity is not required to determine the theoretical shape of the decay curve for a single isotope.
