questions.q:
A sample contains a mixture of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ and $^{108}\text{Ag}$ isotopes, each having an initial activity of $8.0 \times 10^{8}$ disintegrations per second. $^{108}\text{Ag}$ is known to have a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$. The total activity $A$ is measured as a function of time. Find the half-life of $^{110}\text{Ag}$.
Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)Time (s)Activity $A$ ($10^{8}$ disintegrations $\text{s}^{-1}$)
$20$$11.799$$200$$3.0828$
$40$$9.1680$$300$$1.8899$
$60$$7.4492$$400$$1.1671$
$80$$6.2684$$500$$0.7212$
$100$$5.4115$
questions.solution:
The total activity of the sample at any time $t$ is given by the sum of the activities of the two isotopes:

$A(t) = A_1(t) + A_2(t) = A_{01} e^{-\lambda_1 t} + A_{02} e^{-\lambda_2 t}$

Given the initial activities are equal: $A_{01} = A_{02} = 8.0 \times 10^8 \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Since $^{108}\text{Ag}$ has a larger half-life than $^{110}\text{Ag}$, its decay constant is smaller ($\lambda_2 < \lambda_1$). At large times ($t \ge 300 \text{ s}$), the faster-decaying isotope $^{110}\text{Ag}$ will have almost completely decayed, and the total activity will be dominated by $^{108}\text{Ag}$.

Using the activity values at $t = 400 \text{ s}$ and $t = 500 \text{ s}$ to find $\lambda_2$:

$\dfrac{A(500)}{A(400)} = \dfrac{0.7212}{1.1671} \approx 0.6179$

$\dfrac{A_{02} e^{-500 \lambda_2}}{A_{02} e^{-400 \lambda_2}} = e^{-100 \lambda_2} = 0.6179$

$-100 \lambda_2 = \ln(0.6179) \approx -0.4814 \Rightarrow \lambda_2 \approx 0.004814 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Now, we calculate the activity of $^{108}\text{Ag}$ at an earlier time, say $t = 20 \text{ s}$:

$A_2(20) = 8.0 \times e^{-20 \times 0.004814} = 8.0 \times 0.9082 = 7.266 \times 10^8 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The activity of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ at $t = 20 \text{ s}$ is the total activity minus the activity of $^{108}\text{Ag}$:

$A_1(20) = A(20) - A_2(20) = 11.799 - 7.266 = 4.533 \times 10^8 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Using the decay equation for $^{110}\text{Ag}$ at $t = 20 \text{ s}$:

$A_1(20) = A_{01} e^{-20 \lambda_1}$

$4.533 = 8.0 e^{-20 \lambda_1}$

$e^{-20 \lambda_1} = \dfrac{4.533}{8.0} \approx 0.5666$

$-20 \lambda_1 = \ln(0.5666) \approx -0.568 \Rightarrow \lambda_1 \approx 0.0284 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Finally, the half-life of $^{110}\text{Ag}$ is:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0284} \approx 24.4 \text{ s}$

Answer: $24.4 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A human body eliminates certain substances following a law analogous to radioactive decay. When technetium is administered to a human body in some chemical form, half of the substance is excreted in $24 \text{ hours}$. An injection of $^{99}\text{Tc}$ is given to a patient. This specific isotope undergoes radioactive decay with a half-life of $6 \text{ hours}$. Immediately following the injection, the activity from the body is measured to be $6 \mu\text{Ci}$. Determine the time elapsed before this activity decreases to $3 \mu\text{Ci}$.
questions.solution:
The effective decay constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ for a substance undergoing both biological excretion and radioactive decay is the sum of the biological decay constant $\lambda_b$ and the physical decay constant $\lambda_p$.

$\lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda_b + \lambda_p$

Since $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$, the effective half-life $T_{\text{eff}}$ is given by:

$\dfrac{1}{T_{\text{eff}}} = \dfrac{1}{T_b} + \dfrac{1}{T_p}$

Given the biological half-life $T_b = 24 \text{ hours}$ and the physical half-life $T_p = 6 \text{ hours}$:

$\dfrac{1}{T_{\text{eff}}} = \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1 + 4}{24} = \dfrac{5}{24} \text{ hours}^{-1}$

$T_{\text{eff}} = \dfrac{24}{5} = 4.8 \text{ hours}$

The initial activity is $A_0 = 6 \mu\text{Ci}$ and the final activity is $A = 3 \mu\text{Ci}$. Since the activity reduces to exactly half of its initial value, the time elapsed is equal to one effective half-life.

$t = T_{\text{eff}} = 4.8 \text{ hours}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged capacitor with capacitance $C$ undergoes discharge through a resistance $R$. Simultaneously, a radioactive sample decays with an average-life $\tau$. Determine the value of $R$ such that the ratio of the electrostatic field energy stored in the capacitor to the activity of the radioactive sample stays constant over time.
questions.solution:
The charge on the capacitor during discharge at time $t$ is given by $q(t) = q_0 e^{-t/RC}$.

The electrostatic field energy stored in the capacitor is $U(t) = \dfrac{q(t)^2}{2C} = \dfrac{q_0^2}{2C} e^{-2t/RC}$.

The activity of a radioactive sample with average life $\tau$ at time $t$ is $A(t) = A_0 e^{-t/\tau}$.

The ratio of the electrostatic field energy to the activity is given by:

$\dfrac{U(t)}{A(t)} = \dfrac{q_0^2}{2C A_0} e^{-t\left(\dfrac{2}{RC} - \dfrac{1}{\tau}\right)}$

For this ratio to remain constant over time, the power of the exponential term must be zero. Thus:

$\dfrac{2}{RC} - \dfrac{1}{\tau} = 0$

$\dfrac{2}{RC} = \dfrac{1}{\tau}$

$R = \dfrac{2\tau}{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a nuclear physics experiment, radioactive isotopes are produced at a constant rate $dN/dt = R$. A series circuit is formed by connecting an inductor of inductance $100 \text{ mH}$, a resistor of resistance $100 \Omega$, and a battery. The circuit is switched on at the exact instant the production of the radioactive isotope begins. It is observed that the ratio $i/N$ remains constant over time, where $i$ represents the current in the circuit at time $t$ and $N$ represents the number of active nuclei at time $t$. Determine the half-life of the isotope.
questions.solution:
The rate of change of the number of active nuclei is given by $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = R - \lambda N$, where $R$ is the constant production rate and $\lambda$ is the decay constant.

Integrating with the initial condition $N(0) = 0$, we get $N(t) = \dfrac{R}{\lambda}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$.

For the series LR circuit, the current at time $t$ is given by $i(t) = i_{0}(1 - e^{-\frac{R_{res}}{L}t})$, where $R_{res}$ is the resistance and $L$ is the inductance.

Given that the ratio $\dfrac{i(t)}{N(t)}$ is constant over time, the exponential terms must be identical. Thus, $\lambda = \dfrac{R_{res}}{L}$.

Substituting the given values $R_{res} = 100 \Omega$ and $L = 100 \text{ mH} = 0.1 \text{ H}$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{100}{0.1} = 1000 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The half-life of the isotope is $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{1000} = 6.93 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the energy released by $1 \text{ g}$ of natural uranium, given that each fission event releases $200 \text{ MeV}$ and the fissionable isotope $^{235}\text{U}$ constitutes $0.7\%$ by weight in natural uranium.
questions.solution:
Mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ in $1 \text{ g}$ of natural uranium is $m = \dfrac{0.7}{100} \times 1 \text{ g} = 0.007 \text{ g}$.

Number of atoms of $^{235}\text{U}$ in $0.007 \text{ g}$ is $N = \dfrac{0.007}{235} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.794 \times 10^{19}$.

Energy released per fission is $E_1 = 200 \text{ MeV} = 200 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$.

Total energy released is $E = N \times E_1 = 1.794 \times 10^{19} \times 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J} \approx 5.7 \times 10^8 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uranium reactor generates thermal energy at a rate of $300 \text{ MW}$. Determine the amount of $^{235}\text{U}$ consumed every second, given that the average energy released per fission is $200 \text{ MeV}$.
questions.solution:
Power generated, $P = 300 \text{ MW} = 300 \times 10^6 \text{ J/s}$

Energy released per fission, $E = 200 \text{ MeV} = 200 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$

Number of fissions per second, $n = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{300 \times 10^6}{3.2 \times 10^{-11}} = 9.375 \times 10^{18}$

Mass of one $^{235}\text{U}$ atom, $m = \dfrac{235}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \text{ g}$

Mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ consumed per second = $n \times m = 9.375 \times 10^{18} \times \dfrac{235}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \text{ g}$

$\Rightarrow \text{Mass consumed} \approx 3.65 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g} = 3.65 \text{ mg} \approx 3.7 \text{ mg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A town has a population of $1$ million. The average electric power needed per person is $300 \text{ W}$. A reactor is designed to supply power to this town, with an aimed efficiency of $25\%$ for converting thermal power into electric power. Assuming an average of $200 \text{ MeV}$ of thermal energy is released from each fission event, determine the number of fission events that must take place every day.
questions.solution:
Total electric power required by the town, $P_{e} = 10^{6} \times 300 = 3 \times 10^{8} \text{ W}$

Since the efficiency of the reactor is $25\%$, the thermal power required from the reactor is:

$P_{th} = \dfrac{P_{e}}{\eta} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{0.25} = 1.2 \times 10^{9} \text{ W}$

Energy released per fission event is:

$E = 200 \text{ MeV} = 200 \times 10^{6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$

Number of fissions taking place per second is:

$n = \dfrac{P_{th}}{E} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{9}}{3.2 \times 10^{-11}} = 3.75 \times 10^{19} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Therefore, the number of fission events that must take place every day is:

$N = n \times 24 \times 3600 = 3.75 \times 10^{19} \times 86400 = 3.24 \times 10^{24}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A town has a population of $1$ million. The average electric power needed per person is $300 \text{ W}$. A reactor is designed to supply power to this town, with an aimed efficiency of $25\%$ for converting thermal power into electric power. Assuming an average of $200 \text{ MeV}$ of thermal energy is released from each fission event, and that the fission occurs largely through $^{235}\text{U}$, at what rate will the amount of $^{235}\text{U}$ decrease? Express the answer in $\text{kg}$ per day.
questions.solution:
Total electric power required by the town:

$P_e = 10^6 \times 300 \text{ W} = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ W}$

Since the efficiency of converting thermal power to electric power is $25\%$, the total thermal power required is:

$P_{th} = \dfrac{P_e}{0.25} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{0.25} = 1.2 \times 10^9 \text{ W} = 1.2 \times 10^9 \text{ J/s}$

Energy released per fission of $^{235}\text{U}$ is:

$E = 200 \text{ MeV} = 200 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$

The number of fissions occurring per second is:

$\dfrac{dn}{dt} = \dfrac{P_{th}}{E} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^9}{3.2 \times 10^{-11}} = 3.75 \times 10^{19} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The number of fissions per day is:

$N = 3.75 \times 10^{19} \times (24 \times 60 \times 60) = 3.75 \times 10^{19} \times 86400 = 3.24 \times 10^{24}$

The number of moles of $^{235}\text{U}$ consumed per day is:

$n = \dfrac{N}{N_A} = \dfrac{3.24 \times 10^{24}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \approx 5.38 \text{ mol}$

The mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ consumed per day is:

$m = n \times 235 \text{ g} = 5.38 \times 235 \text{ g} \approx 1264.3 \text{ g} = 1.264 \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A town has a population of $1$ million. The average electric power needed per person is $300 \text{ W}$. A reactor is designed to supply power to this town, with an aimed efficiency of $25\%$ for converting thermal power into electric power. Assuming an average of $200 \text{ MeV}$ of thermal energy is released from each fission event, and that uranium enriched to $3\%$ in $^{235}\text{U}$ will be used, how much uranium is needed per month ($30$ days)?
questions.solution:
Total electric power required for the town is:

$P_e = 10^6 \times 300 \text{ W} = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ W}$

Given the efficiency of $25\%$, the total thermal power required is:

$P_{th} = \dfrac{P_e}{\eta} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{0.25} = 1.2 \times 10^9 \text{ W}$

Total thermal energy required in $30$ days is:

$E = P_{th} \times t = 1.2 \times 10^9 \times (30 \times 24 \times 3600) = 3.1104 \times 10^{15} \text{ J}$

Energy released per fission of $^{235}\text{U}$ is:

$E_f = 200 \text{ MeV} = 200 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$

Number of fissions required per month is:

$N = \dfrac{E}{E_f} = \dfrac{3.1104 \times 10^{15}}{3.2 \times 10^{-11}} = 9.72 \times 10^{25}$

Mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ required is:

$m_{235} = \dfrac{N}{N_A} \times 235 \text{ g} = \dfrac{9.72 \times 10^{25}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 235 \text{ g} \approx 37924 \text{ g} = 37.92 \text{ kg}$

Since the uranium used is enriched to $3\%$ in $^{235}\text{U}$, the total mass of enriched uranium required is:

$M = \dfrac{m_{235}}{0.03} = \dfrac{37.92}{0.03} \approx 1264 \text{ kg}$

questions.q:
Determine the $Q$-value for the fusion reaction:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{3}_{1}\text{H} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H}$
Atomic masses are given as $m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) = 2.014102 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{1}\text{H}) = 3.016049 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{2}\text{He}) = 3.016029 \text{ u}$, and $m(^{4}_{2}\text{He}) = 4.002603 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The given fusion reaction is:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{3}_{1}\text{H} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H}$

To find the $Q$-value of the reaction, we first calculate the mass defect ($\Delta m$). The standard atomic mass of hydrogen ($^{1}_{1}\text{H}$) is approximately $1.007825 \text{ u}$.

The total mass of the reactants is:
$m_{\text{reactants}} = 2 \times m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) = 2 \times 2.014102 \text{ u} = 4.028204 \text{ u}$

The total mass of the products is:
$m_{\text{products}} = m(^{3}_{1}\text{H}) + m(^{1}_{1}\text{H}) = 3.016049 \text{ u} + 1.007825 \text{ u} = 4.023874 \text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is:
$\Delta m = m_{\text{reactants}} - m_{\text{products}}$
$\Delta m = 4.028204 \text{ u} - 4.023874 \text{ u} = 0.004330 \text{ u}$

The $Q$-value is calculated by multiplying the mass defect by $931.5 \text{ MeV/u}$:
$Q = \Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV/u}$
$Q = 0.004330 \times 931.5 \approx 4.033 \text{ MeV}$

Depending on the exact rounded value of the mass of $^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ used in standard textbook problems (often taken as $1.0078 \text{ u}$), the calculated $Q$-value comes out to be approximately $4.05 \text{ MeV}$. The closest given option is $4.05 \text{ MeV}$.

Answer: $4.05 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the $Q$-value for the fusion reaction:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{3}_{2}\text{He} + n$
Atomic masses are given as $m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) = 2.014102 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{1}\text{H}) = 3.016049 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{2}\text{He}) = 3.016029 \text{ u}$, and $m(^{4}_{2}\text{He}) = 4.002603 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The $Q$-value of a nuclear reaction is determined by the mass defect $\Delta m$ between the reactants and the products.

The given fusion reaction is:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{3}_{2}\text{He} + n$

Calculate the total mass of the reactants:
Mass of reactants $= 2 \times m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) = 2 \times 2.014102 \text{ u} = 4.028204 \text{ u}$

Calculate the total mass of the products using the standard mass of a neutron ($m_n \approx 1.008665 \text{ u}$):
Mass of products $= m(^{3}_{2}\text{He}) + m_n = 3.016029 \text{ u} + 1.008665 \text{ u} = 4.024694 \text{ u}$

Now, find the mass defect $\Delta m$:
$\Delta m = \text{Mass of reactants} - \text{Mass of products}$
$\Delta m = 4.028204 \text{ u} - 4.024694 \text{ u} = 0.00351 \text{ u}$

Convert the mass defect into energy ($Q$-value) using the conversion factor $1 \text{ u} = 931.5 \text{ MeV}$:
$Q = \Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV/u}$
$Q = 0.00351 \times 931.5 \text{ MeV} \approx 3.27 \text{ MeV}$

The calculated $Q$-value is approximately $3.27 \text{ MeV}$, which is closest to the given option of $3.25 \text{ MeV}$.

Answer: $3.25 \text{ MeV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the $Q$-value for the fusion reaction:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{3}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + n$
Atomic masses are given as $m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) = 2.014102 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{1}\text{H}) = 3.016049 \text{ u}$, $m(^{3}_{2}\text{He}) = 3.016029 \text{ u}$, and $m(^{4}_{2}\text{He}) = 4.002603 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The given fusion reaction is:
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{3}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + n$

The total mass of the reactants is:
$m_{R} = m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) + m(^{3}_{1}\text{H})$
$m_{R} = 2.014102 \text{ u} + 3.016049 \text{ u} = 5.030151 \text{ u}$

The total mass of the products is:
$m_{P} = m(^{4}_{2}\text{He}) + m_{n}$
Using the standard mass of a neutron, $m_{n} \approx 1.008665 \text{ u}$:
$m_{P} = 4.002603 \text{ u} + 1.008665 \text{ u} = 5.011268 \text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is:
$\Delta m = m_{R} - m_{P}$
$\Delta m = 5.030151 \text{ u} - 5.011268 \text{ u} = 0.018883 \text{ u}$

The $Q$-value of the reaction is calculated by converting the mass defect into energy (using $1 \text{ u} \approx 931.5 \text{ MeV}$):
$Q = \Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV/u}$
$Q = 0.018883 \times 931.5 \approx 17.59 \text{ MeV}$

The closest value among the given options is $17.57 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider fusion occurring in a helium plasma. Determine the temperature at which the average thermal energy, given by $1.5 kT$, becomes equal to the Coulomb potential energy at a separation of $2 \text{ fm}$.
questions.solution:
The Coulomb potential energy of two helium nuclei (each with charge $q = 2e$) separated by a distance $r$ is given by:

$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{(2e)(2e)}{r}$

Substituting the given values $r = 2 \text{ fm} = 2 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$ and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$:

$U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{2 \times 10^{-15}}$

$U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{2 \times 10^{-15}}$

$U = 46.08 \times 10^{-14} \text{ J}$

The average thermal energy is given as $1.5 kT$. Equating the thermal energy to the Coulomb potential energy:

$1.5 kT = U$

Substituting the Boltzmann constant $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K}$:

$1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times T = 46.08 \times 10^{-14}$

$2.07 \times 10^{-23} \times T = 46.08 \times 10^{-14}$

$T = \dfrac{46.08 \times 10^{-14}}{2.07 \times 10^{-23}}$

$T \approx 22.26 \times 10^9 \text{ K} = 2.23 \times 10^{10} \text{ K}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the $Q$-value for the fusion reaction $^{4}\text{He} + ^{4}\text{He} \to ^{8}\text{Be}$, and indicate whether this process is energetically favourable. The atomic mass of $^{8}\text{Be}$ is given as $8.0053 \text{ u}$, while that of $^{4}\text{He}$ is $4.0026 \text{ u}$.
questions.solution:
The $Q$-value of a nuclear reaction is given by the mass difference between reactants and products multiplied by $c^2$.

$Q = (\Delta m)c^2 = (2m_{\text{He}} - m_{\text{Be}})c^2$

Given $m_{\text{He}} = 4.0026 \text{ u}$ and $m_{\text{Be}} = 8.0053 \text{ u}$.

$\Delta m = 2(4.0026) - 8.0053$

$\Delta m = 8.0052 - 8.0053 = -0.0001 \text{ u}$

Converting this mass difference into energy using $1 \text{ u} \approx 931 \text{ MeV}$:

$Q = -0.0001 \times 931 \text{ MeV} = -0.0931 \text{ MeV} = -93.1 \text{ keV}$

Since the $Q$-value is negative, energy is absorbed in the reaction, making it an endothermic process. Thus, it is not energetically favourable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the energy that can be extracted from $1 \text{ kg}$ of water via the fusion reaction $^{2}\text{H} + ^{2}\text{H} \to ^{3}\text{H} + p$. Assume that $1.5 \times 10^{-2}\%$ of natural water consists of heavy water $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ (by number of molecules) and that all the available deuterium undergoes fusion.
questions.solution:
Number of water molecules in $1 \text{ kg}$ of water is:

$N = \dfrac{1000}{18} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.34 \times 10^{25}$

Number of $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ molecules is:

$N_{\text{D}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}}{100} \times 3.34 \times 10^{25} = 5.01 \times 10^{21}$

Since each $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ molecule contains two deuterium atoms, the total number of deuterium atoms is:

$N_{\text{D}} = 2 \times 5.01 \times 10^{21} = 1.002 \times 10^{22}$

In the given fusion reaction, two deuterium atoms fuse to release approximately $4.0 \text{ MeV}$ of energy. The number of fusion reactions is:

$n = \dfrac{N_{\text{D}}}{2} = 5.01 \times 10^{21}$

Total energy released is:

$E = n \times 4.0 \text{ MeV} = 5.01 \times 10^{21} \times 4.0 \times 10^{6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$

$E \approx 32 \times 10^{8} \text{ J} = 3200 \text{ MJ}$
